# Synthetic data sets for recoant

<!-- Generated by cmd/gendata. DO NOT EDIT. -->

All data in this folder is generated; it contains no third-party and no personal data. Every data set has a known structure, and most come with tables of that hidden structure (clusters, latent factors, item quality, intents, …), so you can tell how well a recommender should do.

## Format

Every data set is a folder with a signals file and optional tables, all CSV with a header row.

`signals.csv` (or `signals.csv.gz`) has one signal per row:

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| time | RFC 3339 timestamp |
| subject_kind, subject_id | who acted, usually `user` |
| object_kind, object_id | what was acted on: an item, product, movie, article or another user |
| type | signal type: visit, click, dwell, cart, purchase, rating, share, follow, … |
| value | magnitude: dwell time in seconds, star rating, quantity; 1 otherwise |
| session | session ID, may be empty |

Signals map one to one onto `recoant.Signal`. Signals files marked *ordered* are sorted by time; read streams in this order.

Data sets with attributes add `schema.csv` (kind, attribute, type, sensitive; types category, number, set, geo) and `attributes.csv`, a stream of attribute events sorted by time:

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| time | RFC 3339 timestamp |
| kind, id | the entity |
| op | `set` (also to update) or `delete` |
| attribute | the attribute; empty with `delete` deletes the whole entity |
| value | category as is, number, set elements joined by `|`, geo as `lat,lon`; empty with `delete` |

Apply attribute events before signals of the same time.

## Data sets

| Folder | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| [basic](#basic) | Batch recommendation with users and items: the baseline (pure popularity) and the standard set for personalized models (taste clusters). |
| [latent](#latent) | Data generated by low-rank models, for SVD/PCA, matrix factorization, ALS and BPR. The true factors are included. |
| [funnel](#funnel) | Signals of different depth and informativeness, for funnel modeling and learning signal relevance. |
| [stream](#stream) | Streams to read in order, for online and incremental learning: trends, new items and preference drift. |
| [session](#session) | Anonymous sessions, for session-based and next-item recommendation. |
| [relations](#relations) | User–user and entity–entity relations, for user-to-user recommendations and graph models. |
| [attributes](#attributes) | Users and entities with attributes (schema.csv) that change over time as events (attributes.csv), for filters, mutual preferences, deletion and retention. |
| [matching](#matching) | Two-sided markets where both sides decide, for reciprocal matching: the target is mutual likes, not likes. |
| [loading](#loading) | Edge cases and invalid rows for loaders and ingestion. |
| [benchmark](#benchmark) | Large files for performance measurements. |

### basic

#### [basic/zipf-popularity](basic/zipf-popularity)

2000 users draw 25 interactions each from the same Zipf distribution (exponent 1.1) over 1000 items, over 30 days. Each interaction walks down the funnel visit → click → dwell → cart → purchase. There is no personal taste.

**Expected:** Popularity is the best possible model here. Personalized models should not beat it by more than noise; if they do, they overfit. items.csv holds the true rank and expected share of each item.

- `signals.csv`: 109229 signals, ordered by time; types visit, click, dwell, cart, purchase; subjects user; objects item
- `items.csv`: 1000 rows; columns item_id, rank, share

#### [basic/taste-clusters](basic/taste-clusters)

5000 users and 2000 items in 10 taste clusters (user u and item i belong to cluster index % 10). Each user has 20 interactions over 30 days; 85 % stay in the user's cluster, the rest go to a random cluster. Within a cluster, item popularity follows a Zipf law (exponent 1.0). Funnel signals visit → click → dwell → cart → purchase.

**Expected:** Personalized models (item-kNN, user-kNN, matrix factorization) should clearly beat popularity, which ignores the clusters. users.csv and items.csv hold the true clusters; similar items or users should mostly share a cluster.

- `signals.csv`: 218379 signals, ordered by time; types visit, click, dwell, cart, purchase; subjects user; objects item
- `users.csv`: 5000 rows; columns user_id, cluster
- `items.csv`: 2000 rows; columns item_id, cluster, rank_in_cluster

### latent

#### [latent/explicit-ratings](latent/explicit-ratings)

Star ratings (1–5) of 3000 users for 1500 movies over 180 days, like the Netflix Prize. Generated as round(μ + b_u + b_m + p_u·q_m + ε) clipped to 1–5, with μ = 3.6, user biases N(0, 0.3), movie biases N(0, 0.4), rank-10 factors and noise N(0, 0.5). Users rate 20 to 300 movies, chosen with a Zipf popularity bias.

**Expected:** Matrix factorization (Funk-SVD, biased MF, SVD++) and truncated SVD/PCA should recover the rank-10 structure: on this data the true model has an RMSE of 0.55 (noise and rounding), the true biases alone 0.91 and the global mean 1.01. A learned model between 0.55 and 0.91 captures latent structure; the closer to 0.55 the better. users.csv and movies.csv hold the true biases and factors (f1–f10).

- `signals.csv`: 148682 signals, ordered by time; types rating; subjects user; objects movie
- `users.csv`: 3000 rows; columns user_id, bias, f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6, f7, f8, f9, f10
- `movies.csv`: 1500 rows; columns movie_id, bias, f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6, f7, f8, f9, f10

#### [latent/implicit-feedback](latent/implicit-feedback)

4000 users, 2000 items, 30 interactions per user over 60 days. A user picks item i with probability ∝ exp((p_u·q_i + b_i) / 0.5) with rank-8 factors and item biases N(0, 0.5). Better matches go deeper into the funnel: click, dwell time, cart and purchase rise with the affinity σ(p_u·q_i + b_i).

**Expected:** The set for implicit-feedback models: ALS (with confidence from signal strength), BPR and item-kNN should clearly beat popularity. Weighting deep signals (purchase, long dwell) higher than visits should help, because depth carries affinity. users.csv and items.csv hold the true factors (user bias is 0).

- `signals.csv`: 380255 signals, ordered by time; types visit, click, dwell, cart, purchase; subjects user; objects item
- `users.csv`: 4000 rows; columns user_id, bias, f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6, f7, f8
- `items.csv`: 2000 rows; columns item_id, bias, f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6, f7, f8

### funnel

#### [funnel/ecommerce](funnel/ecommerce)

Shopping sessions of 8000 users over 3000 products in 20 categories, 30 days. Every user prefers two categories (50 % and 35 % of views, 15 % random). Every product has a hidden quality q ∈ [0, 1] that sets its funnel: click rate 0.15 + 0.5q, median dwell 15 + 60q seconds, cart rate 0.03 + 0.3q after a click, purchase rate 0.25 + 0.5q after the cart. Signals carry session IDs.

**Expected:** Funnel modeling should recover the product rates in products.csv from the signals (click-through, add-to-cart and conversion per product). Ranking by conversion should beat ranking by raw visit counts when the target is purchases. users.csv holds the preferred categories.

- `signals.csv`: 172459 signals, ordered by time; types visit, click, dwell, cart, purchase; subjects user; objects product
- `users.csv`: 8000 rows; columns user_id, category_1, category_2
- `products.csv`: 3000 rows; columns product_id, category, quality, click_rate, cart_rate, purchase_rate

#### [funnel/signal-relevance](funnel/signal-relevance)

5000 users, 2000 items. Every user has 3 hidden intent items. Days 0–20 are browsing with signal types of different informativeness (visit, click, dwell, share, and pure-noise hover); in days 21–27 users buy 80 % of their intent items. signal-types.csv says how each type relates to intent.

**Expected:** Split at day 21 (2026-01-22) and learn signal relevance with purchase as target: the learned weights should rank share and long dwell highest, then click, then visit, with hover near zero. Recommending the items with the strongest weighted browsing signals should predict the purchases (intents.csv) far better than counting all signals equally.

- `signals.csv`: 397434 signals, ordered by time; types visit, click, dwell, purchase, hover, share; subjects user; objects item
- `intents.csv`: 15000 rows; columns user_id, item_id
- `signal-types.csv`: 6 rows; columns type, informative, description

### stream

#### [stream/trending-news](stream/trending-news)

A news site over 14 days: 10 new articles per hour, 400 reads per hour from 10000 users (heavy and light readers). A read picks an article published in the last 72 hours with probability ∝ attractiveness · 2^(−age / half-life); attractiveness is log-normal, the half-life uniform in 2–24 hours. Reads are a visit and, in 60 % of cases, a dwell signal.

**Expected:** Read the stream in order. Trending (popularity with a half-life of a few hours) should clearly beat all-time popularity at predicting the next hour's reads; all-time popularity keeps recommending stale articles. Most articles are new, so this is also a cold-start test. articles.csv holds the true attractiveness and half-life.

- `signals.csv`: 214741 signals, ordered by time; types visit, dwell; subjects user; objects article
- `articles.csv`: 3360 rows; columns article_id, published, attractiveness, half_life_hours

#### [stream/preference-drift](stream/preference-drift)

Like basic/taste-clusters (3000 users, 1500 items, 10 clusters, 85 % loyalty) over 60 days, but on day 30 (2026-01-31) every user switches to another cluster.

**Expected:** Read in order and evaluate test-then-train. After the switch, models with time decay (short half-life) or drift detection should recover quickly; models without decay keep recommending the old cluster. users.csv holds both clusters of every user.

- `signals.csv`: 197302 signals, ordered by time; types visit, click, dwell, cart, purchase; subjects user; objects item
- `users.csv`: 3000 rows; columns user_id, cluster_before, cluster_after
- `items.csv`: 1500 rows; columns item_id, cluster

### session

#### [session/sequences](session/sequences)

20000 anonymous sessions (subject kind "session") over 2000 items, 30 days. 250 disjoint chains of 4–10 items; a session starts somewhere in a chain and follows it for 3–6 steps, with a 15 % chance per step of jumping to a random item. Every step is a visit, 60 % also a click.

**Expected:** Next-item and session-based models (sequential co-occurrence, session-kNN) should predict the next chain item (chains.csv) for most steps; plain co-occurrence ignoring order does worse, popularity is close to useless.

- `signals.csv`: 144407 signals, ordered by time; types visit, click; subjects session; objects item
- `chains.csv`: 1775 rows; columns chain, position, item_id

### relations

#### [relations/social](relations/social)

4000 users and 2000 items in 8 taste clusters (80 % loyalty, 15 item interactions per user) plus a follow graph: every user follows 5–30 others (signal type "follow", object kind "user"), 80 % of them in the same cluster.

**Expected:** User-to-user recommendations (who to follow) should mostly suggest users of the same cluster (users.csv), both from the follow graph and from similar item interactions. Combining both should beat either alone. Item recommendations can use the follow graph as side information.

- `signals.csv`: 200760 signals, ordered by time; types visit, click, dwell, cart, purchase, follow; subjects user; objects item, user
- `users.csv`: 4000 rows; columns user_id, cluster
- `items.csv`: 2000 rows; columns item_id, cluster, rank_in_cluster

#### [relations/catalog](relations/catalog)

3000 products with relations in relations.csv: every product is in one of 30 categories and by one of 100 brands; about 10 % are accessories of another product of the same brand. 5000 users have 3 favorite brands; 70 % of their 20 interactions go to products of these brands.

**Expected:** Graph models (random walks over user–product–brand) should find the brand preference (users.csv) and recommend unseen products of the favorite brands, also for products with few interactions. Category relations carry no preference signal and should not help much.

- `signals.csv`: 218803 signals, ordered by time; types visit, click, dwell, cart, purchase; subjects user; objects product
- `users.csv`: 5000 rows; columns user_id, brand_1, brand_2, brand_3
- `relations.csv`: 6290 rows; columns subject_kind, subject_id, relation, object_kind, object_id

### attributes

#### [attributes/people](attributes/people)

A people-discovery app: 2500 users sign up in the first 30 days and are active for 120 days. Attributes (attributes.csv, schema in schema.csv): age 20–55, preferred age range min_age–max_age, gender (no influence on behavior), location in one of 5 cities (all at least 150 km apart, users within 15 km of the center) and 3–5 of 20 interests; age, gender and location are sensitive. A user views 20–50 profiles, 85 % in the own city. Like probability σ(−1.2 + 1.2·attractiveness + 0.5·shared interests), ×0.05 outside the user's preferred age range, ×0.2 in another city; 10 % of likes are superlikes; otherwise 70 % pass (1 % of them block). A like that completes a mutual like is followed by a message in 60 % of cases. During the period 20 % change their age preferences, 8 % move to another city, 10 % replace their interests, 3 % delete them, and 6 % delete their account: no signal involves them afterwards.

**Expected:** Filters: {"attribute": "age", "within": ["min_age", "max_age"], "mutual": true} and {"attribute": "location", "max_distance_km": 50} should keep most likes and drop most passes: inside the subject's preferred age range and within 50 km 34 % of views become likes, outside 2 %, about 18 times less; mutual preferences matter for matches, because both sides decide. Apply attributes.csv in time order together with the signals: preferences, locations and interests change, and the user rows (signals, attributes) of deleted accounts must be removed at their deletion time (users.csv). Mutual likes (match) are the target for reciprocal matching (v0.6). With a retention of 60 days on the likes relation, pairs whose last signal is older than 60 days before the end drop out. Gender has no effect: models and filters should not need it. users.csv holds the hidden attractiveness.

- `signals.csv`: 146262 signals, ordered by time; types block, like, message, pass, superlike, view; subjects user; objects user
- `schema.csv`: 6 rows; columns kind, attribute, type, sensitive
- `attributes.csv`: 16678 rows; columns time, kind, id, op, attribute, value
- `users.csv`: 2500 rows; columns user_id, attractiveness, signup, city_at_signup, deleted

#### [attributes/shop](attributes/shop)

A shop over 90 days: 2500 products in 15 categories by 60 brands with a price (log-normal around a median of 10–500 per category), 2–4 of 30 tags and, for 30 %, a pickup store location. 4000 users have a budget min_price–max_price (max = 4.5·min), 3 preferred tags, a location and 2 hidden favorite categories (users.csv). Each user makes 20 visits: 70 % in a favorite category; the product is drawn ∝ exp(0.5·quality + shared tags), ×0.03 outside the budget, and walks down the funnel visit → click → dwell → cart → purchase, with cart and purchase ×0.1 outside the budget. 20 % of the products launch in days 30–90 (attributes at launch, no signals before), 5 % are discontinued in days 45–90, 10 % change their price once, 10 % of the users change their budget once (all in attributes.csv).

**Expected:** The filter {"attribute": "price", "within": ["min_price", "max_price"]} should keep nearly all purchases (99 %) while dropping most products; {"attribute": "tags", "same": true} keeps the products users interact with: 54 % of visits share a tag with the user, against 28 % for a random product. Products launched late have only attributes at first: a cold-start case for feature-based models (v0.10). Discontinued products (products.csv) must be deleted at their time and never recommended afterwards. products.csv holds the hidden quality.

- `signals.csv`: 169685 signals, ordered by time; types visit, click, dwell, cart, purchase; subjects user; objects product
- `schema.csv`: 9 rows; columns kind, attribute, type, sensitive
- `attributes.csv`: 27916 rows; columns time, kind, id, op, attribute, value
- `users.csv`: 4000 rows; columns user_id, category_1, category_2
- `products.csv`: 2500 rows; columns product_id, quality, launch, discontinued

### matching

#### [matching/dating](matching/dating)

A dating app where both sides decide, over 90 days. 3000 users each have a hidden style (one of 6) and prefer one style in others; attractiveness is N(0, 1). Each user views up to 60 profiles: 70 % drawn at random, 30 % weighted by e^attractiveness, as an app that ranks by popularity would. A like is shown to the liked user, who looks at the liker in 50 % of the cases ("who liked you") and decides the same way. Like probability σ(−2 − 0.8·max(own attractiveness, 0) + 0.6·attractiveness of the other + 3·[the other has the preferred style]): attractive profiles get more likes and are pickier. Otherwise 80 % pass. A like that completes a mutual like is followed by a message in 70 % of cases. The most attractive 10 % receive 28 % of all likes; a like to them is returned in 6.6 % of cases, a like to the others in 16.9 %.

**Expected:** The target is matches, not likes: a recommendation succeeds if the user likes the profile and the profile likes the user back. One-way models (popularity, ALS on likes) recommend what the user likes, which includes many attractive profiles who rarely like back; reciprocal matching (recoant v0.6: interest in both directions, combined with a harmonic mean) should raise the mutual hit rate, and exposure balancing should spread recommendations (lower Gini) without losing matches. users.csv holds the hidden style, preferred style and attractiveness: a perfect matcher recommends profiles whose style the user prefers and who prefer the user's style.

- `signals.csv`: 364581 signals, ordered by time; types like, message, pass, view; subjects user; objects user
- `users.csv`: 3000 rows; columns user_id, style, preferred_style, attractiveness, likes_received, likes_given

### loading

#### [loading/edge-cases](loading/edge-cases)

Valid but tricky signals: out-of-order times, an exact duplicate, zero and implausibly long dwell, an unknown type without session, a time zone offset, non-ASCII IDs and IDs with commas and quotes, quantities, fractional and negative values, user → user and item → item signals, a self-loop, far past and future times, and kinds, IDs and types that differ only in case.

**Expected:** Every row must be accepted by ingestion. What happens to each is a policy question (e.g. ignore unknown types, cap dwell time); tests should state it explicitly.

- `signals.csv`: 18 signals; types visit, click, dwell, purchase, Visit, bought_together, follow, rating, return, share; subjects User, item, user; objects Item, item, user

#### [loading/invalid](loading/invalid)

One problem per row: unparseable time, empty subject kind, empty subject ID, empty object kind, empty object ID, empty type, non-numeric value, NaN, infinite value, missing column.

**Expected:** Every row must be rejected with an error; none may panic or be silently accepted.

- `signals.csv`: 10 signals

Like basic/taste-clusters at scale: 200000 users, 50000 items, 100 clusters, 8 interactions per user over 90 days. Gzip-compressed.

**Expected:** For throughput and memory measurements of ingestion, training and recommendation. Quality expectations as for basic/taste-clusters.

## Read the data in Go

This folder is a Go module (`github.com/breskos/recoant-data/synthetic`, standard library only, no dependency on recoant). [catalog.go](catalog.go) lists every data set with its files, [synthetic.go](synthetic.go) reads them, [example_test.go](example_test.go) shows how, and [synthetic_test.go](synthetic_test.go) checks every file against the catalog and its hidden structure:

```
go test ./...
```

## Regenerate

The generators are in [internal/gen](internal/gen). The same seed produces identical files:

```
go run ./cmd/gendata -out .
```
